newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel mourns 73 troops killed in helicopter crash.
newsitem.headline: Israel mourns 73 troops killed in helicopter crash.

text.p: Israeli broadcasters read out names of the dead at hourly bulletins on Wednesday as the Jewish state mourned for 73 soldiers killed in the worst air disaster in its military history.

The cabinet and parliament observed a minute of silence at meetings in the morning hours after the two U.S.-made Sikorsky CH-53 transporters collided on Tuesday while heading to Israeli-occupied Lebanon.
At least 20 victims were buried in funerals throughout the country after rescue workers identified their bodies. There were no survivors.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on a visit to the site of the crash near the Lebanese border on Wednesday, said the soldiers died on a mission to protect Israel.

"The people here know better than any how these soldiers and heroic commanders take risks to protect the residents of the north," he said at the village of Shaar Yishuv, where one of the helicopters fell onto a house. Nobody on the ground was hurt.
"Our quest for peace involves constant sacrifices, constant risks," a grim-looking Netanyahu said as he watched rescue workers search for body parts and personal belongings.

The helicopters were flying to a 15 km (nine mile)-wide occupation zone in south Lebanon that Israel carved out in 1985 to prevent guerrilla attacks. The pro-Iranian Hizbollah group, fighting to expell Israel from Lebanon, said the crash was an act of God.

"We consider what happened a success granted by God...I will use this occasion to express big happiness and ask our people and loved ones to pray to God and thank him," said Hizbollah deputy chief Sheikh Na'eem Qassem.
Israel's army chief Amnon Shahak said in a statement to soldiers that Israeli troops would remain in Lebanon.
"The army is engaged in a never ending war, a drawn-out war to defend the state of Israel on its northern borders and throughout the country," he said.
"The mission grows more and more difficult and sometimes hits too close to home...(but) we will strengthen ourselves and confort ourselves with the belief that the army can overcome this tragedy."

Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai named a five-man committee to investigate the disaster but officials refused to speculate on its cause. Witnesses reported explosions after the helicopters crashed, apparently from ammunition in the cargo.

Israelis, including politicians across the spectrum, mourned the loss of life. Most of the dead were around the age of 20. In Israel's previous worst military air disaster, 54 paratroopers died in a helicopter crash in 1977.

Flags were lowered to half-mast and shops were closed. The official mourning period began on Wednesday at 3 p.m. (1300 gmt) and runs until 7 p.m. (1700 gmt) on Thursday. Religious leaders called for a day of fast and prayer on Thursday.
Netanyahu cancelled meetings with Jordan's King Hussein on Wednesday and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Thursday. An aide to Arafat said the meeting with Netanyahu would take place on Sunday.
Condolences poured in from King Hussein, Arafat, Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and U.S. President Bill Clinton.

The question of Israel's involvement in Lebanon had come up earlier this week when three soldiers were killed by a Hizbollah bomb. Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani complained the soldiers were sitting ducks.
Twenty-seven Israeli soldiers were killed fighting in Lebanon last year.
